utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Usher [sic], good afternoon to you and to everybody. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. I notice all the accused are present. I only notice the absence of Mr. Haynes from the Defence teams. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. I understand, Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Thayer, that you have a short preliminary. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon, everyone. Very briefly, in -- with respect to the protective measures application regarding Witness 49, the Chamber had inquired yesterday as to Witness 49's current profession, and I'll try to stay in open session for this. I didn't have much in the way of particulars. I do now. I think I can share a little bit more, which may or may not bear on the Court's pending decision. I just wanted to bring the information such as it was to the attention of the Court. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you do this in private session. We went through all this already in private session when Mr. Josse was addressing the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Will do, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, let's go into open [sic] session, and just to be on the cautious side let's redact the last -- lines 22 and 23 of page 1. And you can repeat the same in -- or if you need to, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are continuing to speak with Mr. Bourgon and Ms. Nikolic about the Defence expert. I don't think that should be a problem, we'll work out the details with that and we'll give them to you once we have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Bourgon, if you wish to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, president. I am ready at this time to provide the Trial Chamber with some dates that were discussed between all the Defence team and the Prosecution, if you would like me to do so at this time or to wait later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think wait until you hear what we have to say and then of course we will be very extremely interested in hearing what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I apologise to the interpreters. My microphone was switched off. Perhaps it will be useful, on second thought, to hear the result of the ongoing negotiations or consultations between you and the Prosecution. I thank you so much Mr. Bourgon and Mr. McCloskey for having pursued this matter. Also with the utmost celerity after you raised it in one the sittings last week or earlier on this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The idea is the Defence proposes to hear an expert witness in the case of the intercepts. The scope of the report would cover the technical aspects of the intercept-taking exercise, showing that it was simply not possible to intercept the type of conversations being led by the Prosecution into evidence. So this is why, in our view, it goes to admissibility. In order to -- for this to happen, we discussed with the Prosecution and we would agree on following dates we that we propose to the Trial Chamber. The Defence expert report could be ready and filed along with the proper notice by 23 April. Then starting the calendar from 23 April, the witness could testify, depending of course, it would be for the Prosecution to fit that witness into its schedule, we figure that if we go with the 30-day delay, being the minimum delay, the witness could testify as early as 23 May, which would then trigger a filing schedule, the Prosecution being first 20 days later, 21 days later, 13th of June. Followed by Defence submission also 21 days later on the 4th of July. And ending with a Prosecution response 14 days later on the 18th of July. And by that -- by then the Trial Chamber would have, or would be in possession of everything and be able to render a decision on the admissibility of the intercept evidence. Of course, these are just proposed dates and we stand at the -- we will go along with whatever the Trial Chamber in terms of dates. Those are the ones that would fit both the Prosecution and the defence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would there be any problem if we have Prosecution submission before we hear the expert -- Defence expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No problem with us. I think my colleague will disagree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution have asked for four weeks' extension.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We would -- it obviously would be best for us to incorporate a response to the expert. I don't want to be overconfident on this point, but it's not -- may not be absolutely necessary and it could be a chapter that we -- that we throw in afterward. That's the one -- that -- that brings up the one complicated issue, is after their expert are you going to want to hear from anyone else on this topic. You may. I don't know, and given the creativity of this, I don't know if the Defence would object to that, but we may -- we may feel the need to call an expert on that point, though you've heard a number of people in the electronic field that have talked about this issue basically. We haven't gone into the real nuts and electronic bolts of it, but whether we'll need to or not, I don't -- I don't know. We haven't seen what the person has had to say. So that's the only complicated and part and as long as we're -- there's some flexibility to allow us to call someone, if necessary, that that's the only complication I foresee. And we're ready to argue this thing at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But in the meantime, let me think aloud for a moment. Of course there will be consultations. I'm just pointing out to you that if we extend your -- the time limit as per your motion, that would have it extended to the 29th of April, 29th of April. Which would be six days, roughly a week, after the conclusion or the availability of the -- of the expert report. We could -- I -- as I understand, and I fully agree with what Judge Kwon stated. The one-month extension can always remain there fully, with a full understanding that if the expert report raises new issues, you can come back with further submissions in due course, in which case the Defence time limit for the filing of their response will shift forward accordingly. This is also another possibility, but I need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, Mr. McCloskey, we had come prepared, actually, to make an oral ruling on the order -- or on the Prosecution motion today. And in a way we are grateful to both of you, as I said, for having pursued this matter to put us in time, give us the information in time before we can hand our decision. We are making a suggestion, and we invite feedback from you. We would like to know exactly what you think about our proposition. Our proposition is that we will extend the time limit requested by the Prosecution, that is, extending it by a month, and that in other words, will extend to go right to the 29th of April. In your submissions you will address only what we've heard so far. You will not address the issues which will have been raised in the meantime in the report of the -- of the expert. Now, we'll hear the expert sometime around the 23rd of May, as suggested by Mr. Bourgon. After the end of the testimony -- of the expert witness's testimony, you will have two weeks within which to file your response to the Prosecution's submissions. I'm saying "you," Mr. Bourgon, it means all the others, obviously. In the meantime you would have certainly worked on the other aspects involved because you would have received the Prosecution's submissions well ahead in time. After the filing of your submissions, then the Prosecution will have another fortnight, another two weeks within which to file its response, which would of course supposedly cover also, cover also the issues that arise in the wake of the expert witness's testimony. I think, since Mr. Bourgon needs to consult with his colleagues and I suppose you also need some time to think about it, we will postpone our decision until after the first break. In the meantime, if necessary, you can talk. But we are -- it's a proposition that we are making. We would be very much prepared -- we have flexibility -- we would be very much prepared to hear any further submissions that you may wish to make. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Indeed, I would ask for a short delay at least until the next break to discuss with my colleagues to get the Defence -- the position of all Defence teams. However there is one issue I would like to raise at this time, further to what my colleague from the Prosecution mention about the possibility for them to call someone else later. Now, Mr. McCloskey, has said that this course, what we are embarking on now is of course a creative proposal, and the Trial Chamber said yesterday that of course it could not do that unless the Defence was -- voluntarily suggested such an approach. Now, in our view we are willing to put a Defence earlier in time, that is, not wait until the Prosecution has ended its case. However, with respect to intercept, it is our understanding that the Prosecution has finished leading evidence towards admissibility of the intercepts. Because if we're going to do this only to be finding ourselves facing another Prosecution expert, then we would prefer simply to wait for the Defence case. So I would just like to make that clear that if we do such a proposal, to make it easier for the Trial Chamber and easier for all parties that this will be the final matter with respect to admissibility of intercepts. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Bourgon, for having raised that matter. Mr. McCloskey, perhaps you would like to address this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If -- if a technical expert testifies that this cannot be done technically, I don't -- you know, it's hard to anticipate, but having heard from the Muslim experts in this, and everything else, the Prosecution may not feel the need to rebut that, frankly. Because it's, in our view, pretty absurd Defence. But if the Court may not agree with my view of that, it may want to hear something, and perhaps we will need, feel the need that something needs to be rebutted, just as if they'd put that person on in their case, we would be allowed to rebut it. It's hard to imagine that we'll need to do that, frankly, between cross-examination and the evidence that you heard, but it may be something that we would like to do and, in fact, the ultimate test would be to get a series of experts and have them go to the machines and go to the Republika Srpska and go to the mountain top and see if it could be done. I don't think we'll ever need to do that. I don't think you'll want us to do that, but it's -- I will not agree with this programme if there's a door -- if the normal door to rebut is shut, and I don't anyone is suggesting that, but I don't think it would be in our interest to go forward if the door is shut -- the rebuttal door is shut. So that's -- that is my only -- my only point. Also -- well, you'll be -- I'll...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask a question to Mr. Bourgon. If we can hear the Defence case earlier for our convenience, why would we not be able to hear the Prosecution's rebuttal earlier as well? That way it is being done in many civil law countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We were about to do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Along this --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will spare you what I think of certain judicial systems in other countries. However, the idea is simply that we are making this proposal to make it quicker and safer for all parties, and to make it -- to have -- you know with the dates that we have proposed, it's to make it that the rights of all parties in the courtroom are protected. Of course if there is an issue of rebuttal, there can be rebuttal, but at end of the case, because or else, if we do this now, then the benefit that we are trying to achieve will be lost. That's the only argument, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, I said on specific issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rebuttal only on the matter of intercepts. The other thing I want to mention is nothing is stopping you. I mean we have opened the door already in a previous instance. There's nothing stopping you from having your own expert present here in the room assisting you when the Defence expert is testifying, and that's also a matter to take into consideration. We have allowed it, I have allowed it before in previous cases, and I would allow it again repeatedly, if necessary, yeah, only if necessary. But this is again a matter, et cetera. I would suggest that you again have further consultations. If we are in a position, after the first break, to come back with a concrete proposal or crystallise your respective positions, that will help us go forward with our decision. If not, we can even advance it till later, but we need to decide it tomorrow at the latest, because the 29th March dead-line is with us. All right. So that disposes of one of the preliminaries we had in mind to deal with. Now, Mr. McCloskey, yesterday, the 26th was yesterday, wasn't it. Yes. Yesterday Madam Fauveau, on behalf of General Miletic filed her response -- or their response to the Prosecution motion to amend the 65 ter list by adding three documents. But she basically objects to the granting of the motion and further submits, without prejudice, that should the motion be granted then she requires 30 days' time in which to be -- before being able -- before proceeding with her cross-examination. There's one further matter that she raises, that one of the documents that you seek to include in the 65 ter list has already been introduced in the records by the Defence of General Gvero, and that is that it bears Exhibit Number 6D30. So we are inviting you to, if possible, if you are in a position to do so, to respond to her response today. And also, incidentally, if there are any other Defence teams that would like to formally object to the Prosecution motion for the addition of those three documents to the 65 ter list, to speak now. The witness is soon coming to give testimony, and we need to tell you what the position is. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Defence team for Mr. Beara would join that motion in principle, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Likewise for the team for Mr. Nikolic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Basically our position is the same, Your Honour. Of course there are issues at stake here that fit in with the recent certification request from all Defence teams in relation to this matter as a point of general principle. And we would ask the Chamber to bear that in mind. Also of course there is an additional exhibit on that list that doesn't impact at all on Witness 49, but does, in fact, specifically on our client in relation to Sir Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Thayer, I don't know who is going to address this. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we may just briefly respond to Madam Fauveau's filing, I think we might be able ultimately to save a little bit of time. The -- the only question we would have in response to Madam Fauveau's filing is whether there is any basis put forward yet for that length of delay that is requested in the motion. What we are talking about are two very short, but important, videos, which as I stated before, I think run to maximum of 15 minutes of playing time. We've provided the transcripts, the times to the tenth of a second for each of these only four clips, and it's just not clear to me why 30 days is now required to delay the testimony of this witness. He's here, he's ready to testify, he's been here for a few days, and we don't see any need, based on the motion that was filed, for that amount of time. With respect to the third document, that has been translated, it was introduced through one of the Defence cases, it was not translated, it has been translated and it will be distributed when I get back to my desk this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I want to read you clear. Do you still insist in seeking its addition to the -- to the 65 ter list once it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think that's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- already in the in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's been mooted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The understanding is that if it is mooted, you would still -- still since in the records that you would be able to make use of it, just like any other party here in the course of the proceedings. All right. In relation to the objections, the intrinsic substance of the objections of Madam Fauveau and the others as to the -- whether they should be added to the 65 ter list or not, do you wish to state anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Nothing further beyond that those two videos, we believe really will help the Court in its analysis of the testimony and the evidence. The -- the videos do capture what we anticipate several witnesses will testify to. And we believe that it is very compelling evidence of the events on the ground in Zepa during this period of time covered in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. We'll come to that at right moment, now that we are fully informed of your respective positions. You will recall that on the 15th March the -- that we were -- we received a motion from the Defence teams of Vujadin Popovic, Ljubisa Beara, Drago Nikolic, Ljubomir Borovcanin, and Vinko Pandurevic, seeking clarification of the Trial Chamber's decision regarding Prosecution Rule 94 bis notice which was handed down on the 6th of March of this year. The joint motion requests the Trial Chamber to clarify whether its 6th March, 2007 decision regarding the Prosecution's Rule 94 bis notice should be read as disposing of, "The notice on behalf of Vinko Pandurevic and Drago Nikolic, pursuant to Rule 94 bis (B) filed on the 30th November 2006 or the addendum to Popovic Defence Rule 94 bis notice regarding Prosecution expert witness Richard Butler, which was filed on the 16th of January, 2007 regarding the ability of the proposed Prosecution witness Richard Butler to testify as an expert or regarding the admissibility of his reports." We are deciding this issue orally now. It is the position of the Trial Chamber that our 6th March 2007 decision regarding the Prosecution Rule 94 bis notice should not be read as disposing of any challenge to the ability of the proposed Prosecution witness, Richard Butler, to testify as an expert or to any challenge to the admissibility of his reports raised in the Pandurevic and Nikolic notice of 30th November 2006 or the Popovic addendum of 16th January 2007. I hope that clarifies the matter. In going it over, we didn't really feel that it needed clarification, especially since we gave an extension. But in any case, this is our final word on the matter, and we are confirming that the doors are open, as per our 6th March decision. Yes, I think we can bring in the witness now. Mr. Ostojic, before he comes in, or by the -- while he is ushered in, how much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Approximately 45 minutes to an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have already been two hours 14 minutes, Mr. Ostojic. And we have been dealing with some matters repetitively, and it's our hope that you will try to avoid repetition of that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when you want to be cooperative, you always are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, but try to keep it --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- as short as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. You are still testifying pursuant to the solemn declaration that you made on the first day of your testimony that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Ostojic is going to continue and finish with his cross-examination. And then he will be followed by others. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday we left off discussing your first purported contact and conversation with Mr. Beara, and you had claimed that at that time he had inquired about the machines and the possibility of burying the dead in the Milici municipality. Am I correct, sir, that based on the testimony you gave on Friday, that it was you, sir, who deterred him or stopped him from going to the Milici municipality? When I say on Friday, that was the 23rd of March, page 16, lines 8 through 11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what happened, but I'm not sure that I was the one who stopped Colonel from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned the gentleman also last Friday, Mr. Rajko Dukic who -- and can you just tell us briefly what his role was in the municipality of Milici in 1995? And it's the same cite, it's on page 16, line 16, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 16, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is, because we're still using -- I didn't get a copy of the corrected transcript, and last Friday we had a problem, so they started from page 1 of Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 1 starts from -- with this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I now understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, who Mr. Rajko Dukic, what role he played in the Milici municipality in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what he did, but at the time in Milici, as today, Rajko Dukic is everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we also heard evidence yesterday that there's a mine in Milici. Do you know the name of that mine company in Milici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bauxite mine?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, that mine in Milici, am I correct, sir, that that was a mine that was the best-equipped company, as far as machinery and excavators would be in all of north eastern Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, is it illogical and unbelievable that someone would ask you for machines if, in fact, they were going to bury people in the Milici municipality at that time? Isn't that illogical?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it is illogical or logical, I don't know. In any case, Colonel Beara mentioned this to me. I told him that we did not have machinery for such jobs, that we had a small SKIP and two lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that it would not be logical for us to go to a different municipality and do what he was asking me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Three years ago when you testified in the Blagojevic case, another Defence counsel asked that very question, sir, (redacted) (redacted) and he asked you if it was illogical for someone to be asking you for machines if they were going to bury people in the -- where the mine which had better equipment, and you answered yes, in the affirmative, and today you don't know if that's illogical? Can you just reconcile that for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not logical. Of course it's not logical to go and look for machinery, knowing that there were machines up there. I don't know whether the Colonel knew about my machinery or not until the moment I told him what I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it was because the machinery and equipment belonging to the mine was superior to that what was at your disposal. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the second conversation that you purportedly had with Mr. Beara, which was approximately one or 2.00, I think that you stated. Sir, at that time you said that you went with a military policeman and took a ride to look for the burial site, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that we went to look for a place. I went with the policeman with the intention for them showing me where the place was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought you told us the other day and Friday that the military policeman that you went with was not from Bratunac, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I -- how long was the car ride that you were with this military policeman who you don't know his name, how long were you in the car with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Bratunac to Glogova it takes anything between five and 10 minutes. Five at the most, not longer. It depends on the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And he was driving or you were driving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you -- during that five or 10-minute drive, did you ever have any conversation with this military policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. We must have exchanged a few words, but I don't know what about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would think so as well. At any time did you try to obtain his name, sir, while you were in the car with him alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at any time during that five or 10-minute car ride, did this person who was not from Bratunac seem to you to know where he was going, not having been from the area, or did you, sir, direct him as to where he should go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was driving. I did not have to tell him where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you came to this site, Glogova, did you get out of the car at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what did you do, sir, when you left the car with this military police officer at Glogova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First he turned the car around. Then we got out of the car and then he pointed his finger towards a place and he told me, "This is where you're going to dig a pit."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what time of day was it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. But what time approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, sir, what you did, if anything, after he pointed to the area where you should dig a pit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? What do you mean? You mean at that moment or...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Exactly at that moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. We returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. At that time, sir, were you ever at the area of Glogova where the pit was ultimately buried [sic] by you and your men? Were you ever there prior to that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have used that road before the new road was built, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when was the new road built?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the 1970s when it was opened for traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Sir, I suggest to you that it's illogical and unbelievable that you would go with a military policeman whose name you claim you don't know, who you never saw before in Bratunac, who was not from the Bratunac area and that he would take you to an area five to 10 minutes outside of Bratunac in order to select a pit to bury the dead, and I think, sir, it was you who actually took the military police officer if it happened at all the way you suggested it did. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I have met with more than 500 people over a period of three to four years. I worked with them, they never asked me what my name was, I never asked them what their name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you then to narrow it down. Don't you find it somewhat illogical that was the military police officer who you didn't recognise from Bratunac where you testified as to your background in that town, that he would be taking you as opposed to you taking him to where this purported pit would be dug?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what would make it more logical. I was not in charge. I did not want to do that. I could not choose the localities for burials. Maybe that policeman had been taken there before he took me there. I've told you, I did not choose the place, nor would I have done it, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, I'd forgot to ask you in the beginning, did you discuss your testimony with anyone since you concluded it yesterday afternoon? Whether it be a little bit or extensively, with anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Sir, I want to move to another topic. And it relates to the information you claim you had about people detained in the soccer field. Now, in your interview with Mr. Ruez on the 13th of October, 2000, you stated on page 23, line 7 through 14, that you, "Had no information about people detained in the soccer field on July 12th, 1995 in Bratunac." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And under oath here today you still stand by that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You also told Mr. Ruez on the 13th of October, 2000, same reference, page and line, that there was no army present that night whatsoever. Is that still correct today, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I saw, when I was in front of the municipality building, there were military -- there were civilian policemen, and no army. There could have been troops, but not where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And also, sir, is it correct that you told Mr. Ruez, 13th of October 2000, that you had no specific recollection of the situation in Bratunac the night of the 13th of July, 1995? And the reference for that for my colleague is page 26, lines 11 through 13? Isn't that what you told Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what it says, I must have said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would be easier if you showed him the paragraph and you then, instead of putting the question, you put it -- you ask him whether he confirms having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just in the interests of time we were trying to short circuit it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Also, I think we need to take into account, for clarification, the witness, what he's previously testified about the dates, and how the dates he gave Mr. Ruez were not correct. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, on page 26, lines 11 through 13, Mr. Ruez on the 13th of October, 2000, asked you the following question, "Do you have specific recollection of the situation in Bratunac that night of 13 the of July?" And your answer sir was, "No." Do you remember giving him that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you still, sir, today, under oath stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably said this, but I believe that this is the fifth time that I am saying to you that the dates that I offered during the interview in Banja Luka are not correct. It is obvious I made a lot of mistakes in the dates that I mentioned in that statement. So please don't dwell upon those dates that I offered in Banja Luka. I've already admitted my mistake and I've already apologised for that mistake several times over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, help me clarify it then. Instead of using dates, let's take these time-lines that we've established in this case, although perhaps still debated between the parties. Did you have no specific recollection of the situation in Bratunac before or after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. What situation in Bratunac before the fall or after the fall of Srebrenica? I'm not clear what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'll try to clarify it. You had told Mr. Ruez that you had no specific recollection of the situation in Bratunac. What period of time were you talking about, sir? Although he mentions a date, you were uncertain about the dates. Help me understand, when you told Mr. Ruez you had no specific recollection of the situation in Bratunac, what period of time were you thinking about? Wherein you had no specific recollection.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I was...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are being educated in French. So I think we need -- shall we try again and we will see what is the situation. Because I can only hear myself at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll put the question to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's okay now because otherwise we would have -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters did not get all of your answer to my question. You started to say, "I can't remember." And I just want to. What else did you say, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said I couldn't remember, and I don't know which period I was talking about. I don't know which dates I mentioned to Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Help me with this: During the critical period immediately after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, including the time that you witnessed the incident at Kravica, did you at any time see any personnel from the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw the excessive behaviour in Kravica, you want to know whether I saw member of the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac, that's your question, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not quite, but I will accept that if you want to answer that for me. But let me restate the question, if I may. I don't know why if we're having so much trouble, and it's my fault, I'm sure. Sir, in Bratunac 1995 July, all I'm using is the milestones of actual facts that have been established with the fall of Srebrenica, the incident at Kravica, did you at that time, sir, notice any military personnel from the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw those killings in Kravica I wasn't in Bratunac, and I couldn't see members of the Bratunac Brigade then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Did you ever go back to Bratunac after you saw that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But after a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Any members of the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. And as far as I know, those soldiers from the Bratunac Brigade were at the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And those were at the positions outside of Bratunac, correct? Meaning out the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the interests of time, let me move on to another topic. You had mentioned some buses in front of the municipality building that you saw in July of 1995. Do you generally remember testifying about that in the other case and in your interview with Mr. Ruez? Your Honour, I'm being informed that he did not receive any translation to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will repeat the question slowly. Are you receiving interpretation of what I am saying now, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I am going to read out the question that Mr. Ostojic put to you a few seconds ago. And then you please try to answer it. Let us move on to another topic. "You had mentioned some buses in front of the municipality building that you saw in July of 1995. Do you remember generally remember testifying about that in the other case and during your interview with Mr. Ruez?" Let's start with the interview with Mr. Ruez. Do you remember mentioning that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in your previous testimony, do you remember referring to this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he's back to you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell this Court, sir, what you saw in connection with these buses in front of the municipal building in Bratunac in July 1995. Tell me how many buses you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was with Mr. Srbislav Davidovic who, at the time was the president of the Executive Board of the municipal assembly of Bratunac. I was in his office. We heard the engines of vehicles. When we went out of the building we saw three buses at the very entrance to the municipality building. They were full of people. I can't remember whether there was one or two policemen in uniforms, civilian policemen. Some people were asking for water, and since my office is some 20 or 30 metres from the municipality building, I had some canisters for water, five and 10-litre canisters. So I went to fetch some water, and the president of the Executive Board, Mr. Srbislav Davidovic, and I poured water in the municipality building into the canisters and gave this water to the people in the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when did this happen, sir? And if you don't know the date, use a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening hours. In the evening hours. It was one day before I saw the incident in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So was that the same day or a day after you had this purported meeting with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could just go into private session to give a page reference and then we could jump right back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, approximately three years ago when you gave testimony under oath in another case you had referenced these same buses and this purported meeting with Mr. Beara, and you said at that time, sir, that you're not sure, but you think it was that night when you had the meeting with Mr. Beara. Can you reconcile for me, sir, how three years ago you were not sure, but today you seem to think that the chronology is that you saw those buses the day before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. In this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In this, on line -- on the line he gave us, the witness said he didn't know. So I don't know, he may have said I'm not sure as well somewhere, but apparently he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the very next line, on the very next page, the question is, "Could you tell us whether that was before or after the night when you had your meeting with Colonel Beara." The answer was, "I'm not sure, but I think that it was that night when I had the meeting." And it is specifically page seven -- I gave it to him already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In either case it's -- the way he has worded the question is not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the question, if I may reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I confer with my colleagues, actually he did premise his question on exactly the way his previous reply to Mr. Ruez or -- sorry, to his previous reply in his testimony reads, at least as has been read by Mr. Ostojic, and the question is can you reconcile to me how three years ago you were not sure but today you seem to think that the chronology is that you saw those buses the day before. Do you have an explanation to this or for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when testifying in the Blagojevic case, if I had been certain, I would have said it was that evening, before or after the meeting with Colonel Beara, I wouldn't have said I'm not certain. So I said it was that evening when I analysed everything and prepared myself for this testimony, I came to the conclusion, and realised that it was that day -- or rather, the evening before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this question: Do you remember about the time in 1999 or 2000, when newspapers were giving out articles spreading rumours about Mr. Beara and his purported involvement relating to Srebrenica? Do you recall that at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember at all discussing those newspapers with Mr. Ruez on October 13th, 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was that I mentioned General Beara. He asked me how do you know he's a General? I said I thought that I had read about that somewhere or had seen something to that effect on television. That was our discussion about the newspapers and about television.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you believe, sir, as you sit here that that was your entire discussion about the newspapers and that was -- came from you about what you may have seen on television relating to Mr. Beara's rank? Is that what you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just a minute ago I told you what I told Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, on page 32 of your interview with Mr. Ruez, commencing -- actually, on page 31, I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's page 31. It's a long-winded question that was starting on line 18 through 26. And then proceeding on page 32 of that same interview, line 1 through 6: "Do you remember Mr. Ruez talking to you about the activities on Glogova site, between the 14th and 19th of July, 1995," and then he tells you on line 5 of page 32, "Because I had also -- then talking about Colonel Beara, he's in all the newspapers." Do you remember discussing that with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Obviously you wouldn't then remember your answer. Here is what your answer was, sir, to that discussion, and if the Court wishes, I could read the entire page or so of the question that Mr. Ruez put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you first ask him whether he thinks if you read out his -- this to him, it would -- could refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, would -- if I were to read out your answer to the discussion you had with Mr. Ruez, would that help you remember that discussion at all? Would it refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I jumped the gun, but I'll read it. I think my learned friend probably wants me to read the whole thing and if the Court will -- it starts on page 31, line 18. Mr. Ruez says as follows, sir: "I must inform -- I must just also inform you that until now we are talking about the bodies --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "I must just also inform you that until now we are talking about the bodies alongside of the road. So, bodies that the people who have little knowledge about the situation in this area could believe are combat casualties. When I talk about the bodies found, I mean killed inside the warehouse marked with D on the sketch. We are talking already about a massive war crime. I noted that you were throwing a doubt on the existence of these events. You said if ever people have been killed inside. If you can tell you for sure yes -- " I'm sorry -- "I can tell you for sure yes, bodies have been killed. People have been killed inside, and I even add that we are currently digging out these bodies from the Glogova site that you guys dug in. When I disclose you the information that we have a document from military police of the Bratunac Brigade securing your personnel on that site on the 19th, only someone who knows nothing about the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac town would not know that we are talking about people under the command of Momir Nikolic. So, I'm going to ask you again, what do you know about the activities on Glogova site between the 14th and the 19th July, 1995? Because I had also then talking about Colonel Beara. He's in all the newspapers." Your answer which appears on page 32, line 7 through 10, is as follows: "I'm trying to recall what was happening between the 14th and the 19th, but I fail. Actually, I cannot conceive that my people actually working there for eight days, because it sounds very long for me. Maybe the operator on the machinery was there, but as for the others, I can't imagine that they were there." Do you remember giving that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that at that time, when Mr. Ruez was interviewing you, there were rumours in the newspapers about Mr. Beara and you and Mr. Ruez actually discussed those newspaper articles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having discussed those articles with Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me turn to another subject that you touched upon in your testimony last Friday, and it's on page 10 of the old transcript, lines 4 through 7. When you had this purported first -- or your prior contact with Mr. Beara. We know that you've established when you claim you had first met him in the SDS offices that evening that you've already testified to. Sir, isn't it true, though, that to Mr. Ruez when you were asked if you had ever seen Mr. Beara prior to that contact purportedly in the SDS offices, that you told him that you had seen him that year, not a day or two earlier, but simply that year? Isn't that true? Do you remember telling him that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember telling him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I know that I saw Colonel Beara two or three days prior to our meeting. I think it was then one day later. We met on two or three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We heard your testimony on when you claimed you saw him after your contact with him. On page 9, sir, of your October 13th, 2000 interview, the question on line 8 and 9 was as follows, and they're talking immediately prior to that about Mr. Beara. It says, "Do you remember when you saw him, meaning Mr. Beara, in Bratunac or Bratunac area for the first time? Was it that year?" Your answer, which commences immediately after that on page 9, lines 10 through 12, is as follows: "So I think that I saw him first time that year. Whether he was coming or not prior to that, I wouldn't know, because I hadn't had any kind of dealings with the army, you know, except in extreme cases like the one in question." Do you remember telling Mr. Ruez that in October 2000, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I said that, I think it was connected to those events, not to the beginning of the year. So then it would seem as if it was a long time ago. Those were the days that I had in mind, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Help me understand this, sir: Do you know why would purportedly a military officer from the Main Staff request a meeting with a civilian such as yourself, to be held in a politician's offices such as Mr. Deronjic's in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why they requested this in 1992, that's what I'm asking you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think that, sir, is a question that I'm not allowed to answer, but I think with other witnesses that will come through. Don't you find it quite illogical, sir, that a military officer would call you, a civilian, who wasn't even in the civilian protection defence, such as Mr. Ilic that we talked about, to inquire of you of any machines or of anything whatsoever? Don't you find that illogical?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doesn't seem to be so to me, because until duties were transferred to Ljupko Ilic, I worked throughout the wartime period, and I knew all the officers, I would receive orders from officers, from 1992 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me see, if I may with the Court's permission, 65 ter number 1553, please. I think that was the document that was shown to you by my learned friend. And there's too one that the witness I believe marked, but we can have a clean copy. And it has a P number, if that will help. If we could just enlarge it a bit. Sir, that's a picture that you were asked questions about last Friday. Can you point to the Court where the Bratunac military barracks was in July of 1995 or I should say their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've got to blow it up for that question to be fair -- I mean, shrink it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, would you like me to blow it up or shrink it down or keep it the same, maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if it is blown up a little bit it will be better. As it is, it may be difficult for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If he knows, Your Honour. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's got to be blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's got to be made bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have had other photos of the same town, concentrating on a particular section of the town where it would be more easy for the witness to identify. I don't know, but let's -- let's -- I cannot indicate myself which part to blow up. So -- because that would be involving myself in what I shouldn't be involving myself in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand, and we could -- I have just one final question for him. It's okay. We'll get it with the other witness, Your Honour. We understand the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I definitely think it -- do you think -- Witness, do you think you can identify the Bratunac military barracks or the headquarters on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command was in the Kaolin factory in one of the barracks. Where volunteers were billeted was in the old construction school behind the Vuk Karadzic School.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's where you've placed a little marking there on that document, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's marked the old school, but if he's going to be shown a photograph of the Kaolin -- or the Bratunac Brigade, I think it's only fair that the brigade be in that photograph. It's not currently in this photograph, I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just briefly reply. That's why I thought we had an understanding we're not going to show witnesses pictures with pre-marked areas such as the one that was shown, although it didn't really matter in that case, but we were just asking him if he could identify it and if he couldn't, we would move on; if he did, as he did, he shows it, it's not acceptable for some reason to the Prosecutor. I'm not sure why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are making a storm in a teacup. The suggestion of Mr. McCloskey was not to show him a marked photograph but to just show him a photo and ask him whether he recognises and then move from there, because with this map as it is, one can easily get confused. I mean, we've been to Bratunac, all of us, and if you asked me to mark it, I would find it very difficult. And we have seen the space as well. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It goes to two things, Your Honour. One, this person obviously being from the area and being intimately involved, and secondly, on the credibility of the witness's testimony here where he identifies certain things, can have some impact. But if that -- if the Court wants a bigger picture, we would then move on to another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed any further, I mean I believe we've heard you well. You are suggesting, Mr. McCloskey, that the witness is being shown a photo and being asked to indicate on that photo a particular building or complex of buildings, when you know that that complex of buildings does not show in this -- does not appear in this photo, is that your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then our position is that you should never show a witness a map or a diagram -- or a photo like this asking him to point on it the place that you are suggesting to him, if that place does not exist on that map or on that photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it actually does exist --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if that's fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It does exist on this exhibit, but the way the thing is zeroed in on it now doesn't show it exists. And I -- you know...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to take off his earphones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- just so I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't exist in what we are looking at on the monitor, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It exists on the document but not on what we are -- okay. So I take that back, but we'll have a break. We need to zoom out, then in a way -- or then focus on the area. Please liaise with Mr. McCloskey and decide which part of the photo to be shown to the witness, because I don't want the witness to be shown a photo, at least as it appears on the screen, asking him to mark a place that doesn't show on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It wasn't meant to be a trick question, Your Honour, if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not saying it was meant to be a trick question. I'm saying that we wouldn't accept the situation where the witness is supposed to look at this and mark us a place when we all know, you included, that although the place exists in the photo in its whole size, its entire size, it does not -- it is not included in what is appearing on the monitor. So sort that out amongst yourselves. We will have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to conclude your cross-examination the earliest, please, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was trying -- yes, Mr. President. I was trying to conclude it before the last break, and I will try to that as soon as possible. Just to follow up, if I may, on this picture, we have with the assistance of the Prosecution's case manager, we'd like to call -- or put on the ELMO a document that's not marked but that the Court has in its evidence, which is P02103 and it's page 272 of that book of pictures the Court received earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this in front of the Witness is a blank copy, Mr. President, of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm showing you a picture essentially of what purports to be the Bratunac town, an aerial view. Can you, looking at that picture, and you can look at it either directly or on the screen, tell us where the Bratunac Brigade headquarters was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the factory of the ceramic tiles, isn't it? Can I turn this around, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. If I may interrupt, Mr. President, if he's having that much trouble, we can move on or whatever the Court wishes. I don't want to take up...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will ask him myself. Witness, do you think you have found, identified where the Bratunac Brigade headquarters were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. This is the factory of ceramic tiles. And the command of the brigade was in its administrative building.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with the Court's permission, if he can just mark that exhibit where he believes that it is and that would be adequate with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can write BBH. BBH. No. On -- on the spot where he said -- mark it with an X where he thinks that the Bratunac Brigade headquarters were. He first needs to mark with an H [sic] and then write BBH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mark with an X.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he's -- Witness, look at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Can you bear with me. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And write BBH, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the -- at some part, one of the sides, if you could write PW-161, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]. I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 161. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, thank you, and that's all we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, shall we forget the other photographs where he put an X?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, because I have to just clean up something that he said that wasn't captured in his testimony on page 37, line 16 through 58, and we believe or I believe that the witness used the word "volunteers" and that's where he marked an X that there were volunteers were in the old construction school behind the Vuk Karadzic School. And I just want him to confirm that first, Your Honour, but that's what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You put the question, or rather if he has received interpretation, he can tell us. Is he on the video mode where he can see the map, the photograph that we had before where he marked the X? Yeah. What does that X represent on that photo near -- you put an X in red near a site where previously it stated it's the old school. What's that X supposed to denote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the old construction school where volunteers were billeted, the troops that volunteered to come to Bratunac but did not hail from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So could I ask you now, please, to put P -- to write P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we need to forget about this. Upload it again. He will put the X again in the same place and then we can... Yeah. Now I think he can put a PW-161 on it. And we'll save this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, my last topic, if I may proceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have been already -- when we started it was three hours, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's a very minor topic. It was in response to the witness's answer on page 36, line 2, Your Honour. And I'm just following up on that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, but please conclude in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, earlier today when I asked you the question of why would purportedly a military officer from the Main Staff request a meeting with a civilian such as yourself to be held in the political offices such as Mr. Deronjic's in July of 1995, your answer that appears on page 36, line 2, was, "Why they requested this in 1992. That's what I'm asking you now." I just want to clarify to follow up on that, sir. Who do you mean when you say, "Why they requested this in 1992." Who is the "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already in 1992, and I meant the officers from whom I received orders then, as well as in 1995, when it came to the burial of those who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And tell me, which officers are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 the mass grave that was excavated below the Drina bridge, some 1500 metres downstream of the Drina, it was an officer from Serbia, from the OG Drina Gucevo. They called him Captain Dragan. He took me to the spot, he told me where to dig. We went to the hangar, we saw the bodies. He told me how to load them on to the vehicles, and from then on, this continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Who is next? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many hours, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just for 10 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You see, Mr. Ostojic, you should take example from Mr. Zivanovic. Go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. First of all, let me ask you this: The circumstances which led to you appearing as a witness, in other words, how did you come in contact with Mr. Ruez in 2002? Actually, did you get a formal invitation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That formal invitation was in Serbia, in the language that you understand, I suppose. Can you remember whether in this letter, in this invitation, it said that you were obliged, that you were duty-bound to respond and there were some sanctions mentioned if you didn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this in an envelope and it was the chief of the public security station in Bratunac who gave this envelope to me. It was strictly confidential. I don't remember whether there was any threat. The only thing that was stated was that they guaranteed my safety on the journey from Bratunac to Banja Luka and back for the next five days, and after that, they could not guarantee my safety. This is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One small correction for the transcript. On page 44, line 24, here it says that the formal invitation was in Serbia, and my colleague said in Serbian, in the language that understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So how did you understand this, the five days that you were guaranteed safety on the journey to Banja Luka and back? How did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I understood it. I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask anybody to explain to you what this meant, that you were guaranteed safety for five days and not after that? Did you ask what this meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that during that period of time I was a witness and after that I could have been a suspect or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But in any case, you did not ask anybody to explain, to tell you what this was all about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It said strictly confidential. I didn't dare talk to anybody about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you talked to Mr. Ruez, did he tell you that you were not duty-bound to provide your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you under the impression that you were obliged to provide this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I am going to ask you to explain one thing for me. We've heard that refugees in Potocari were provided with water that was brought in some cisterns. Do you maybe know whether such vehicles were borrowed from your company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that our vehicles were involved in that. I'm not sure. In any case, nobody ever asked me to provide such vehicles for bringing water to the refugees in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could this have been done without you knowing about this? We've heard from some witnesses that you yourself mentioned that cisterns from Bratunac were used, among others, to deliver water, drinking water, to the refugees in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not done with my approval. This cistern was in Kravici [as interpreted], in Sandici, where there were the highest number of people, Muslim refugees who were provided with water. I don't know anything about Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you another thing. To my learned friend Ostojic's question, you said you saw three buses in front of the municipal building on a day, and you can't recall the date. I have read your previous testimony in the other case, which I'm not going to mention, but you know what I'm referring to. And you said in that case that those buses were loaded with children, women and elderly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw women and children in the buses on the road from Bratunac to Kravica and Konjevic Polje. What I saw in front of the municipal building were buses with only men in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why in the previous case you stated that those were women, children and elderly men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was due to a confusion in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was confused. And I got confused on many things when I saw buses driving from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje. I thought I'd seen them, but, no, they were not there. The fact is that they were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But now you are clear on that, your head is clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my head is clear. The picture is absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have also told, before this Trial Chamber -- [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... For a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Mr. Stojanovic, any time you need to go into private session, please let us know. How long do you estimate your cross-examination to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe I'll need between 40 and 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll put some questions to you in order to try and clarify some of the dilemmas that appeared after your testimony on Friday and yesterday. On Friday when testifying, you said that when passing through the village of Kravica by the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje, you saw the execution of five men carried out by one man in a green camouflage uniform. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us at what time in the afternoon it was on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was summertime, but it was in the late afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that on that occasion you did not get out of the vehicle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let's have a look at Exhibit P01564, a Prosecution Exhibit. The ERN number is 0046-1251. And it's one of the photographs of the Kravica warehouse. We've already seen it. While waiting for it to appear on the screen, sir, if you look at the monitor you will see the photograph of the Kravica warehouse and of the road from Bratunac to Kravica and Konjevic Polje. Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that this is, in fact, the Kravica warehouse that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that this is the road you used on that occasion in the late afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the assistance of the usher, could we provide the witness with a marker so that he can mark certain items. Sir, could you please use the marker to mark the spot where you saw the execution you mentioned. Mark it with a cross.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] It's just a little closer to this hangar, at edge of this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This can be erased, so please try to be a little more precise, if possible. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you said that to the right of the site where these men were executed, you saw a pile of bodies. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark with a circle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The location in which you saw those bodies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-161 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've marked a spot on the grass again, but the bodies were between the grass and the hangar, or rather they were on this asphalt surface.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, one moment. Before we proceed, because otherwise it starts getting complicated then. Now, Witness, to the left of that X can you write 5K, 5K.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And to the right of the circle could you please write BD.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].
